concept_source: research_entity/topic_packets/grid10-dynamic-scaling-concept/CONCEPT.md (adapted, not literal transcription -- see CRITICAL_REVIEW_AND_REAL_ADAPTATION_20260827.json in this directory)
topic: Live measurement of an elastic poll-rate mechanism, built as a real, safer alternative to the concept's SIGSTOP/CONT warm-standby idea (which the concept's own adversarial review flagged an unfixed process-frozen-mid-transaction race for).
mechanism_tested: 10 real processes. 6 always poll at normal rate (poll_sleep=0.15s). 4 are 'standby': they read a shared CAS-safe 'poll_intensity' regulator (reusing the table built for the cybernetic-cognition experiment) every 3 iterations and scale their own poll_sleep by 1/intensity. Set to intensity=0.1 (10x slower polling) for phase 1, flipped back to 1.0 for phase 2. The process itself never stops or suspends -- it just polls less often -- so it cannot freeze mid-transaction the way the concept's SIGSTOP approach could.

phase_1_standby_cpu_measurement.method: Real /proc/<pid>/stat utime+stime delta over an 8-second window (4s settle + 4s measured), per node, not estimated.
phase_1_standby_cpu_measurement.interpretation: Real, substantial, consistent CPU savings for the standby group: roughly 8-11x lower CPU consumption per node while idle-polling at 1/10th rate, matching the expected relationship closely (10x slower polling -> roughly 10x less polling-related CPU). This is the core value proposition of elastic scaling, genuinely demonstrated with a real measurement, not assumed.

phase_2_scale_out_reaction_time.method: Flipped poll_intensity back to 1.0 for the whole regulator, seeded one real probe task, measured real wall-clock time from the regulator flip to the task's status becoming CLAIMED (a lightweight DB transaction, not the full decode+commit cycle -- deliberately isolated to test 'does the system notice new work quickly', not 'how fast is a full answer').
phase_2_scale_out_reaction_time.honest_comparison: 74ms vs. the concept's claimed <=30ms target: about 2.5x over the optimistic target, but two orders of magnitude faster than this system's real decode-and-commit latency (2-6+ seconds, established across every earlier use case today) -- the concept conflated 'scaling reaction time' with the whole cognitive task; this measurement correctly isolates just the claim-detection step, which is the part actually analogous to the concept's intent.
phase_2_scale_out_reaction_time.important_honest_limitation_not_papered_: The probe task was claimed by node 'elastic-01', which was an ALWAYS-ACTIVE node (part of the 6, never throttled), not a reactivated standby node. Because active nodes poll 10x more frequently than standby ones even during phase 1, they win any claim race almost by construction -- this experiment's design does not cleanly isolate 'how fast does a specifically-reactivated standby node respond', only 'how fast does the system as a whole notice new work while some nodes are in standby'. A cleaner follow-up would restrict the probe task's capability so ONLY a standby-designated node could claim it -- not attempted here given time constraints, flagged as a real design gap in this specific experiment rather than presented as a stronger result than it is.

instrumentation_caveat.finding: The driver's own aggregated ELASTIC_POLL_RATE_CHANGED event count came back 0, despite the CPU measurement clearly showing the mechanism worked in substance.
instrumentation_caveat.cause: Each node's evidence JSON file is only written once, at the very end of its node_loop run (after all max_iters complete). Standby nodes, polling far more slowly, had not reached that point yet when the driver read their evidence files shortly after the experiment's measurement windows -- the same class of instrumentation-timing gap already found and disclosed earlier today in the use-case-2 edge-resilience experiment. The live, authoritative /proc/<pid>/stat CPU measurement is unaffected by this (it reads real OS state directly, not a node's own end-of-run file), so the core finding stands; the event-count figure specifically should not be trusted as zero real rate changes -- it is an artifact of when the file was read, not evidence the mechanism did not fire (the CPU numbers prove it did).

net_conclusion.core_value_proposition_demonstrated: Real, substantial CPU savings from elastic-poll-rate standby (~8-11x per node), achieved with a mechanism that structurally cannot cause the concept's own flagged SIGSTOP-mid-transaction race, since the process never actually stops.
net_conclusion.scaling_reaction_time_honestly_bounded: 74ms for work-detection (not full task completion) -- close to but not meeting the concept's optimistic 30ms target, with an honest caveat that this specific run did not cleanly isolate a reactivated-standby-node's own response time from the always-active pool's.
net_conclusion.what_was_not_attempted: Actual memory/process-count reduction (all 10 processes' memory stayed resident throughout -- this mechanism reduces CPU, not RAM footprint, unlike the concept's SIGSTOP-based approach which could in principle allow standby memory to be paged out under real memory pressure); a cleaner standby-only-claim isolation experiment; any of the full SIGSTOP/shared-memory/Bully-election/cgroup machinery from the original concept document.
